title: Elusive and real
hookLine: the Tao is shadowy and elusive, yet within it is something real (Tao Te Ching 21)

lines: HARD TO PIN, HARD TO DOUBT.
cards: The wind can't be held in a hand. What you get is the evidence: a flag snapping on a pole, a field of grass bending all one way, a door that slams on its own.

You can't point at the thing itself, and yet nobody standing in a gale thinks it's imaginary. Some solid things in a life work like that: trust between two old friends, the pull of a place you grew up.
Hard to pin down, and hard to doubt. Chapter twenty-one of the Tao Te Ching describes the Way in exactly that double sense.

teach.b: First, virtue follows the Way. The chapter opens by saying that the shape of great virtue comes from following the Tao, and the Tao alone.
Whatever goodness looks like, its source is this thing the chapter is about to describe.
Second, shadowy and elusive. The description is slippery on purpose. The Chinese uses a pair of words, huang and hu, that suggest something dim, flickering, glimpsed out of the corner of an eye.
You look, and it slips out of sight. You reach, and it isn't where your hand lands.
Third, something real inside. Then the turn. Within that dimness, the chapter says, there are forms.
Within it, there are things. Deep and dark as it is, there is an essence in it, and that essence is very real. There is even something trustworthy in it, a kind of proof.
Elusive is not the same as empty.

teach.h: HOW DO I KNOW? BY THIS.
teach.b: Fourth, how do I know? By this. The chapter ends with the speaker asking how he knows the way all things began.
His answer is two words: by this. No argument. He points at what's in front of him, the world as it is, as if the evidence were the flag and the grass.
Some readers hear a quiet confidence in that: you can't hold the Way, but you can live in its weather.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching sit with chapter twenty-one's paradox: the Way can't be grasped or seen, yet the text insists there is something real and trustworthy within it.

o: dim and hard to grasp, yet true at its center
a feeling that seems real but is only imagined
simple and obvious once you finally study it

s: chapter twenty-one says the Tao is elusive, so there is nothing in it
it says the opposite: within the dimness there are forms, things, and a very real essence.
the chapter ends with a long argument proving the Tao
it ends with two words: by this. the speaker points instead of arguing.
the chapter says great virtue follows the Tao
its opening line: the shape of great virtue comes from following the Tao alone.

games.q: you're the speaker of chapter twenty-one. someone asks how you know the way all things began. what do you say?
o: lay out a careful proof, step by step.
admit it can't be known at all.
say "by this," and point at the world in front of you.
games.why: the chapter's answer is just "by this." no proof, no shrug: the evidence is what's already here.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you rely on without being able to show it to anyone: that a certain person means well, that rest will help, that morning will come.
Don't defend it; just lean on it for a minute, the way you'd lean on a wall you can't see in the dark. If you pray, this may be a place for that; if you don't, the leaning is enough.

wordCard.voice: Elusive and real. Chapter twenty-one's picture of the Way: dim and slippery to the hand, with something true and trustworthy at its center. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese, huǎng hū: dim, flickering, elusive. Tao Te Ching 21 uses it for the Way.

carryVoice: Your line: something real. Hard to measure is not the same as unreal. Rest well.
